title: Heat stroke (adults and children)
subject: emergency
summary: Core temperature above 40 degrees C with CNS dysfunction after heat exposure or exertion is heat stroke: cool first, transport second. Start whole-body cooling within 30 minutes (cold-water immersion for exertional cases, evaporative plus ice for frail classic cases) to 38 to 39 degrees C, then support failing organs. Antipyretics do not work.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Heat stroke: core temperature above 40 degrees C (104 degrees F) with CNS dysfunction (confusion, delirium, ataxia, seizures, coma) after heat exposure or exertion. Skin may be hot and dry, but sweating often persists in exertional heat stroke.

Exertional: young, active people (labourers, farm workers, athletes, soldiers), sporadic. Classic: elderly, infants, chronically ill and those on heat-sensitising drugs, in epidemics during heatwaves.
Heat exhaustion: weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, vomiting, cramps, temperature below 40 degrees C and NO CNS involvement; can progress to heat stroke.
Measure core temperature with a rectal probe inserted at least 10 cm; oral, axillary, tympanic and forehead readings are unreliable. Never delay cooling to find a thermometer.

Differentials (start cooling while evaluating): cerebral malaria, meningitis or encephalitis, sepsis, anticholinergic or sympathomimetic toxicity, serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, thyroid storm, hypoglycaemia, exercise-associated hyponatraemia, stroke.

sections.title: Cool first, transport second
items: Begin whole-body cooling immediately, at the scene or on arrival, and within 30 minutes of presentation; aim for a cooling rate of at least 0.15 degrees C per minute.

Exertional heat stroke: cold or ice-water immersion is the gold standard. Immerse trunk and limbs to the neck in water about 2 to 15 degrees C (colder is better), stir the water continuously, and place an ice-wet towel over head and neck.

Classic heat stroke in elderly or comorbid patients, or when immersion would hinder monitoring: spray or mist the whole undressed body with lukewarm water under a strong fan, plus ice-wet towels (NPCCHH). ERC 2025 advises the fastest available method, such as cold-water immersion.
Ice packs to neck, axillae and groin alone cool too slowly; use them only as an add-on. Air conditioning alone is not adequate.

Stop active cooling at a core temperature of 38 to 39 degrees C (38.3 to 39 for exertional) to avoid overshoot; do not cool below 38 degrees C. Without a thermometer, stop when shivering starts or after about 15 minutes of immersion.
Do not delay cooling to remove clothing; undress while cooling. Protect the airway, give oxygen, obtain IV access and check glucose and sodium at the bedside.

sections.title: Supportive care
items: Fluids: IV crystalloid in small boluses with frequent reassessment; many patients are not severely depleted and elderly patients are prone to pulmonary oedema. Children in shock: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg, reassess, repeat to a total of 60 mL/kg.
Seizures or excessive shivering: short-acting benzodiazepine (lorazepam IV). If intubated, neuromuscular blockade abolishes shivering.
Do NOT give paracetamol, NSAIDs or aspirin (ineffective in heat stroke and may worsen liver, kidney and clotting injury). Dantrolene is not recommended.
Intubate for falling GCS, persistent seizures or airway compromise; ventilate with lung-protective settings.
Treat hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis (fluids for good urine output, renal replacement if needed); give blood products for bleeding with DIC; ICU for multi-organ dysfunction.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Glucose, sodium, potassium, calcium, phosphate, urea and creatinine, CK and urine myoglobin, liver enzymes (peak around 48 hours; jaundice at 36 to 72 hours), CBC, PT/INR, fibrinogen and D-dimer, ABG with lactate, ECG, troponin.

Malaria rapid test or smear, blood cultures if infection is possible; CT brain if CNS dysfunction persists after cooling or there are focal signs; lumbar puncture if meningitis cannot be excluded (after cooling and a clotting check).
Repeat CK, creatinine, liver enzymes and coagulation at least daily for the first 72 hours, because organ injury often peaks after cooling.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Continuous rectal (or oesophageal) temperature during cooling, then every 15 to 30 minutes to detect rebound hyperthermia or overshoot hypothermia.
Vital signs, GCS, ECG (arrhythmias), urine output; watch for pulmonary oedema, AKI, liver failure and DIC over the next 24 to 72 hours.
Recheck glucose and potassium often in the first 24 hours (hypoglycaemia; hyperkalaemia from rhabdomyolysis or AKI).

sections.title: Disposition and follow-up
items: Admit all heat stroke; ICU for persistent CNS dysfunction, shock, respiratory failure, AKI, liver injury or DIC.
Heat exhaustion: rest in a cool place, oral rehydration with salt-containing fluids (ORS, lassi, nimbu pani); discharge when well with normal mentation, admit if not improving.
After heat stroke: review 7 days after discharge with repeat tests of affected organs; no exercise for at least 7 days, then re-acclimatise gradually over 2 to 4 weeks.
Report suspected heat stroke cases and heat-related deaths through the NPCCHH heat-related illness surveillance as per state protocol.

sections.title: Children, elderly and pregnancy
items: Children: same cooling priority, but do not overcool (hypothermia can be fatal); seizures: lorazepam 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg IV (maximum 4 mg); shock: 20 mL/kg boluses up to 60 mL/kg with checks for fluid overload.
Elderly: evaporative cooling is better tolerated; mortality stays high despite cooling; give fluids cautiously.
Pregnancy: heat stroke threatens mother and fetus; cool rapidly, use left lateral tilt, and involve obstetrics for fetal monitoring.

sections.title: Prevention (heat season)
items: Public advice: avoid going out in the sun between 12 noon and 3 pm, avoid strenuous afternoon activity, drink water often, wear light loose clothing, check on elderly people living alone, never leave a child in a parked vehicle.
Workers: shaded rest breaks, water and ORS access, heavy work scheduled for cooler hours, and gradual acclimatisation for new or returning workers.

Hospitals: set up a cooling area before summer (ice, tubs, cold water, fans, rectal thermometers) and train staff; review medicines that impair heat tolerance (diuretics, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, beta blockers).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Transporting before cooling, or relying on ice packs and fans in a hot ambulance.
Using oral or axillary temperature and missing heat stroke, or stopping cooling too early.
Giving antipyretics, or labelling fever with coma as heat stroke without testing for malaria and meningitis.
Overcooling below 38 degrees C, or excessive IV fluid in the elderly.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: Adult 4 mg IV (0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg); child 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg IV over 2 to 5 minutes (maximum 4 mg); may repeat once
drugs.notes: Seizures or excessive shivering during cooling. Watch for respiratory depression.

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.dose: Adult 10 mg IM if no IV access (5 mg if 13 to 40 kg)
drugs.notes: Seizures when IV access is not available.

drugs.name: Crystalloid (0.9% saline, Ringer lactate)
drugs.dose: Adult: small boluses with reassessment; child in shock: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg, repeat to a total of 60 mL/kg
drugs.notes: Watch for pulmonary oedema, especially in the elderly. Continue maintenance fluids after shock is corrected.

drugs.name: Dextrose
drugs.dose: Adult: 25 g IV (100 mL of 25% or 250 mL of 10%); child: 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV
drugs.notes: If glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L); recheck in 15 minutes.

drugs.name: Oral rehydration solution (ORS)
drugs.dose: Sip frequently as tolerated for heat exhaustion
drugs.notes: Only if fully alert and able to swallow.
